# Incident Report — NetSupport RAT Infection
**Case:** mta-2024-11-26 traffic-analysis-exercise
**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-11-26-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (21,281,925 bytes), `2024-11-26-traffic-analysis-exercise-alerts.txt` (Suricata/ET alert export)
**Analysis tool:** tshark (`/opt/homebrew/bin/tshark`)

## 1. Victim host

| Attribute | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.11.26.183** | Consistent source IP across all traffic below |
| MAC address | **d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b** (Intel NIC OUI) | Ethernet headers, frames to/from 10.11.26.3 and external hosts |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-B8TQK49** | NBNS: `DESKTOP-B8TQK49<00>` (Workstation), `<20>` (Server service), source 10.11.26.183 |
| Logged-in domain user | **oboomwald** | Kerberos AS-REQ, `kerberos.CNameString = oboomwald`, exchanged between 10.11.26.183 and the domain controller 10.11.26.3 (frames 213, 221, and AS-REP frames 223/235/275/279/298/421) |
| AD domain | NEMOTODES (NetBIOS) / nemotoads.health (DNS), DC = 10.11.26.3 (NBNS name NEMOTODE-DC / DNS name NEMOTODES-DC.nemotoads.health) | NBNS + Kerberos realm fields + DNS SRV/LDAP lookups |

The default gateway/DNS server/DC for the LAN is 10.11.26.3 (MAC 00:24:e8:7f:09:5d).

Note: SMB/NTLM Suricata hits between 10.11.26.183 and 10.11.26.3 (SMBv1, EfsRpcOpenFileRaw, "NTLMSSP overflow attempt", "TRANSACTION DOS attempt") correspond only to routine Group Policy retrieval — `GptTmpl.inf` and `Registry.pol` under `\nemotodes.health\Policies\{31B2F340-...}\Machine\` were exported cleanly via SMB — and are not part of the malicious activity. These are known noisy legacy GPL rules that fire on benign domain-joined SMB traffic.

## 2. Malware family

**NetSupport RAT** (malicious repurposing of the legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-control client).

**Attribution: signature-confirmed**, on two independent grounds observed directly in the capture:
1. The client identifies itself with the literal HTTP User-Agent string **`NetSupport Manager/1.3`** on every C2 request (e.g., frames at 67.39s, 67.59s, 67.89s onward, POST `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm`).
2. Suricata/ET fired protocol-specific signatures matching the known NetSupport RAT C2 pattern: `ETPRO TROJAN NetSupport RAT CnC Activity`, `ETPRO TROJAN Malicious NetSupport Rat CnC Checkin`, `ET INFO NetSupport Remote Admin Checkin/Response`, and `ET POLICY NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request` — all against the same session.

The C2 protocol body observed in the POST payloads follows NetSupport's known beacon format: `CMD=ENCD\nES=1\nDATA=<encrypted blob>`.

## 3. Indicators of compromise (all observed directly in this capture)

**Command-and-control:**
- **194.180.191.64:443** — primary C2. Traffic is plaintext HTTP (not TLS) tunneled over port 443 (flagged by ET as "HTTP traffic on port 443 / Possibly Hostile"). Beacon URI: `POST http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm`, ~60-second interval, from first check-in at **04:50:45 UTC** through the end of the capture (last observed ~04:50:45 UTC + ~3231s ≈ 05:44 UTC).

**Supporting/staging infrastructure:**
- **geo.netsupportsoftware.com → 104.26.1.231** — NetSupport's own geolocation lookup (`GET /location/loca.asp`), queried by the RAT immediately after installation (04:50:32 UTC relative / t=67.2s) to geolocate the victim (returned coordinates `33.7488,-84.3877`). ET rule: `NetSupport GeoLocation Lookup Request`.

**Likely delivery-chain domains** (visited immediately before infection, in this order, all resolved/contacted by the victim):
- **classicgrand.com → 213.246.109.5** (t=32.8s)
- **modandcrackedapk.com → 193.42.38.139** (t=35.7s, then again at t=37.3s and t=62.1s) — flagged by ET as a `ZPHP Domain` in both DNS lookup and TLS SNI (`ET CURRENT_EVENTS ZPHP Domain in DNS Lookup/TLS SNI (modandcrackedapk .com)`)
- **confirmsubscription.com → 52.8.34.0** (t=35.7s, t=37.3s)
- **css.createsend1.com / js.createsend1.com → 18.160.156.x** (t=37.7s)

These four domains form a redirect/gate chain (malvertising or fake "crack download" page) that the victim traversed in the ~30 seconds before the NetSupport client appeared on the wire. All sessions to modandcrackedapk.com were TLS 1.2/1.3-encrypted, so **no plaintext file was captured** at this stage — I cannot ground a dropped file name or SHA256 hash in the traffic. A Windows SmartScreen application-execution check (`checkappexec.microsoft.com`, t=59.6s) and an Authenticode OCSP/CRL check (`r10.o.lencr.org`, t=62.3s) occur in this window, consistent with the user launching a signed downloaded executable, but the binary itself is not recoverable from this pcap.
- No file transfer with recoverable name or hash was observed anywhere else in the capture (HTTP export objects were all small text/`.htm`/`.php`/`.asp` C2 artifacts; SMB export objects were only GPO files; no PE/`MZ` header signature was found in any TCP payload).

**Malicious URL:**
- `http://194.180.191.64/fakeurl.htm` (C2 beacon endpoint, POST, repeated)

## 4. Summary

Workstation DESKTOP-B8TQK49 (10.11.26.183, MAC d0:57:7b:ce:fc:8b), logged in as domain user `oboomwald` (NEMOTODES/nemotoads.health domain), browsed through classicgrand.com → confirmsubscription.com/createsend1.com trackers → modandcrackedapk.com (ET-flagged ZPHP domain) starting at 04:49:52–04:50:14 UTC. An executable was fetched and run over that encrypted session (SmartScreen/OCSP checks at 04:50:29–04:50:32 UTC). By 04:50:45 UTC the host was running NetSupport RAT, confirmed by its own User-Agent string and matching ET/Suricata signatures, beaconing every ~60 seconds to **194.180.191.64:443**. No cleartext dropped file or hash could be extracted from this capture; the infection vector's payload was fully TLS-encrypted.
